entries.2924dc62dc1306d8e3a585647e9dbbf653fee73b: <div sID="gen11778" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="73" osisID="Ps.73" sID="Ps.73"/> <div eID="gen11778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11779" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11780" type="x-p"/> This psalm, and the ten that next follow it, carry the name of Asaph in the titles of them. If he was the penman of them (as many think), we rightly call them psalms of Asaph. If he was only the chief musician, to whom they were delivered, our marginal reading is right, which calls them psalms for Asaph. It is probable that he penned them; for we read of the words of David and of Asaph the seer, which were used in praising God in Hezekiah's time, <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.30">2 Chron. xxix. 30</reference>. Though the Spirit of prophecy by sacred songs descended chiefly on David, who is therefore styled "the sweet psalmist of Israel," yet God put some of that Spirit upon those about him. This is a psalm of great use; it gives us an account of the conflict which the psalmist had with a strong temptation to envy the prosperity of wicked people. He begins his account with a sacred principle, which he held fast, and by the help of which he kept his ground and carried his point, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">ver. 1</reference>. He then tells us, I. How he got into the temptation, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.2-Ps.73.14">ver. 2-14</reference>. II. How he got out of the temptation and gained a victory over it, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.15-Ps.73.20">ver. 15-20</reference>. III. How he got by the temptation and was the better for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.21-Ps.73.23">ver. 21-23</reference>. If, in singing this psalm, we fortify ourselves against the life temptation, we do not use it in vain. The experiences of others should be our instructions.
entries.c5cfd346e8a6e8541bbd24bc95138395e8398ba7: <div eID="gen11780" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11779" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Goodness to His People; Unsanctified Prosperity.</title> <div sID="gen11781" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Truly God <hi type="italic">is</hi> good to Israel, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to such as are of a clean heart. <hi type="super">2</hi> But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. 3 For I was envious at the foolish, <hi type="italic">when</hi> I saw the prosperity of the wicked. <hi type="super">4</hi> For <hi type="italic">there are</hi> no bands in their death: but their strength <hi type="italic">is</hi> firm. <hi type="super">5</hi> They <hi type="italic">are</hi> not in trouble <hi type="italic">as other</hi> men; neither are they plagued like <hi type="italic">other</hi> men. <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; violence covereth them <hi type="italic">as</hi> a garment. 7 Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish. <hi type="super">8</hi> They are corrupt, and speak wickedly <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> oppression: they speak loftily. <hi type="super">9</hi> They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth. <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore his people return hither: and waters of a full <hi type="italic">cup</hi> are wrung out to them. <hi type="super">11</hi> And they say, How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High? <hi type="super">12</hi> Behold, these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase <hi type="italic">in</hi> riches. <hi type="super">13</hi> Verily I have cleansed my heart <hi type="italic">in</hi> vain, and washed my hands in innocency. <hi type="super">14</hi> For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning. <div eID="gen11781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11782" type="x-p"/> This psalm begins somewhat abruptly: <hi type="italic">Yet God is good to Israel</hi> (so the margin reads it); he had been thinking of the prosperity of the wicked; while he was thus musing the fire burned, and at last he spoke by way of check to himself for what he had been thinking of. "However it be, yet God is good." Though wicked people receive many of the gifts of his providential bounty, yet we must own that he is, in a peculiar manner, good to Israel; they have favours from him which others have not. <div eID="gen11782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11783" type="x-p"/> The psalmist designs an account of a temptation he was strongly assaulted with—to envy the prosperity of the wicked, a common temptation, which has tried the graces of many of the saints. Now in this account, <div eID="gen11783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11784" type="x-p"/> I. He lays down, in the first place, that great principle which he is resolved to abide by and not to quit while he was parleying with this temptation, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">v. 1</reference>. Job, when he was entering into such a temptation, fixed for his principle the omniscience of God: <hi type="italic">Times are not hidden from the Almighty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job xxiv. 1</reference>. Jeremiah's principle is the justice of God: <hi type="italic">Righteous art thou, O God! when I plead with thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer. xii. 1</reference>. Habakkuk's principle is the holiness of God: <hi type="italic">Thou art of purer eyes than to behold iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab. i. 13</reference>. The psalmist's, here, is the goodness of God. These are truths which cannot be shaken and which we must resolve to live and die by. Though we may not be able to reconcile all the disposals of Providence with them, we must believe they are reconcilable. Note, Good thoughts of God will fortify us against many of Satan's temptations. <hi type="italic">Truly God is good;</hi> he had had many thoughts in his mind concerning the providences of God, but this word, at last, settled him: "For all this, God is good, <hi type="italic">good to Israel, even to those that are of a clean heart.</hi>" Note, 1. Those are the Israel of God that are of a clean heart, purified by the blood of Christ, cleansed from the pollutions of sin, and entirely devoted to the glory of God. An upright heart is a clean heart; cleanness is truth in the inward part. 2. God, who is good to all, is in a special manner good to his church and people, as he was to Israel of old. God was good to Israel in redeeming them out of Egypt, taking them into covenant with himself, giving them his laws and ordinances, and in the various providences that related to them; he is, in like manner, good to all those that are of a clean heart, and, whatever happens, we must not think otherwise. <div eID="gen11784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11785" type="x-p"/> II. He comes now to relate the shock that was given to his faith in God's distinguishing goodness to Israel by a strong temptation to envy the prosperity of the wicked, and therefore to think that the Israel of God are no happier than other people and that God is no kinder to them than to others. <div eID="gen11785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11786" type="x-p"/> 1. He speaks of it as a very narrow escape that he had not been quite foiled and overthrown by this temptation (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But as for me,</hi> though I was so well satisfied in the goodness of God to Israel, yet <hi type="italic">my feet were almost gone</hi> (the tempter had almost tripped up my heels), <hi type="italic">my steps had well-nigh slipped</hi> (I had like to have quitted my religion, and given up all my expectations of benefit by it); <hi type="italic">for I was envious at the foolish.</hi>" Note, 1. The faith even of strong believers may sometimes be sorely shaken and ready to fail them. There are storms that will try the firmest anchors. 2. Those that shall never be quite undone are sometimes very near it, and, in their own apprehension, as good as gone. Many a precious soul, that shall live for ever, had once a very narrow turn for its life; almost and well-nigh ruined, but a step between it and fatal apostasy, and yet snatched as a brand out of the burning, which will for ever magnify the riches of divine grace in the nations of those that are saved. Now, <div eID="gen11786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11787" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us take notice of the process of the psalmist's temptation, what he was tempted with and tempted to. <div eID="gen11787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11788" type="x-p"/> (1.) He observed that foolish wicked people have sometimes a very great share of outward prosperity. He <hi type="italic">saw,</hi> with grief, <hi type="italic">the prosperity of the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.3">v. 3</reference>. Wicked people are really foolish people, and act against reason and their true interest, and yet every stander-by sees their prosperity. [1.] They seem to have the least share of the troubles and calamities of this life (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">They are not in the troubles of other men,</hi> even of wise and good men, <hi type="italic">neither are they plagued like other men,</hi> but seem as if by some special privilege they were exempted from the common lot of sorrows. If they meet with some little trouble, it is nothing to what others endure that are less sinners and yet greater sufferers. [2.] They seem to have the greatest share of the comforts of this life. They live at ease, and bathe themselves in pleasures, so that <hi type="italic">their eyes stand out with fatness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">v. 7</reference>. See what the excess of pleasure is; the moderate use of it enlightens the eyes, but those that indulge themselves inordinately in the delights of sense have their eyes ready to start out of their heads. Epicures are really their own tormentors, by putting a force upon nature, while they pretend to gratify it. And well may those feed themselves to the full who have <hi type="italic">more than heart could wish,</hi> more than they themselves ever thought of or expected to be masters of. They have, at least, more than a humble, quiet, contented heart could wish, yet not so much as they themselves wish for. There are many who have a great deal of this life in their hands, but nothing of the other life in their hearts. They are ungodly, live without the fear and worship of God, and yet they prosper and get on in the world, and not only are rich, but <hi type="italic">increase in riches,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.12">v. 12</reference>. They are looked upon as thriving men; while others have much ado to keep what they have, they are still adding more, more honour, power, pleasure, by increasing in riches. <hi type="italic">They are the prosperous of the age,</hi> so some read it. [3.] Their end seems to be peace. This is mentioned first, as the most strange of all, for peace in death was every thought to be the peculiar privilege of the godly (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">Ps. xxxvii. 37</reference>), yet, to outward appearance, it is often the lot of the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">There are no bands in their death.</hi> They are not taken off by a violent death; they are foolish, and yet die not as fools die; for <hi type="italic">their hands are not bound nor their feet put into fetters,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.33-2Sam.3.34">2 Sam. iii. 33, 34</reference>. They are not taken off by an untimely death, like the fruit forced from the tree before it is ripe, but are left to hang on, till, through old age, they gently drop of themselves. They do not die of sore and painful diseases: <hi type="italic">There are no pangs,</hi> no agonies, <hi type="italic">in their death, but their strength is firm</hi> to the last, so that they scarcely feel themselves die. They are of those who <hi type="italic">die in their full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet,</hi> not of those that <hi type="italic">die in the bitterness of their souls and never eat with pleasure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.23">Job xxi. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.21.25">25</reference>. Nay, they are not bound by the terrors of conscience in their dying moments; they are not frightened either with the remembrance of their sins or the prospect of their misery, but die securely. We cannot judge of men's state on the other side death either by the manner of their death or the frame of their spirits in dying. Men may die like lambs, and yet have their place with the goats. <div eID="gen11788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11789" type="x-p"/> (2.) He observed that they made a very bad use of their outward prosperity and were hardened by it in their wickedness, which very much strengthened the temptation he was in to fret at it. If it had done them any good, if it had made them less provoking to God or less oppressive to man, it would never have vexed him; but it had quite a contrary effect upon them. [1.] It made them very proud and haughty. Because they live at ease, <hi type="italic">pride compasses them as a chain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.6">v. 6</reference>. They show themselves (to all that see them) to be puffed up with their prosperity, as men show their ornaments. <hi type="italic">The pride of Israel testifies to his face,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">Hos. v. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Isa. iii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Pride ties on their chain,</hi> or necklace; so Dr. Hammond reads it. It is no harm to wear a chain or necklace; but when pride ties it on, when it is worn to gratify a vain mind, it ceases to be an ornament. It is not so much what the dress or apparel is (though we have rules for that, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9">1 Tim. ii. 9</reference>) as what principle ties it on and with what spirit it is worn. And, as the pride of sinners appears in their dress, so it does in their talk: <hi type="italic">They speak loftily</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.8">v. 8</reference>); they affect <hi type="italic">great swelling words of vanity</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2 Pet. ii. 18</reference>), bragging of themselves and disdaining all about them. Out of the abundance of the pride that is in their heart they speak big. [1.] It made them oppressive to their poor neighbours (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Violence covers them as a garment.</hi> What they have got by fraud and oppression they keep and increase by the same wicked methods, and care not what injury they do to others, nor what violence they use, so they may but enrich and aggrandize themselves. <hi type="italic">They are corrupt,</hi> like the giants, the sinners of the old world, when <hi type="italic">the earth was filled with violence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.11">Gen. vi. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.13">13</reference>. They care not what mischief they do, either for mischief-sake or for their own advantage-sake. <hi type="italic">They speak wickedly concerning oppression;</hi> they oppress, and justify themselves in it. Those that speak well of sin speak wickedly of it. <hi type="italic">They are corrupt,</hi> that is, dissolved in pleasures and every thing that is luxurious (so some), and then they deride and speak maliciously; they care not whom they wound with the poisoned darts of calumny; from on high they speak oppression. [3.] It made them very insolent in their demeanour towards both God and man (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">They set their mouth against the heavens,</hi> putting contempt upon God himself and his honour, bidding defiance to him and his power and justice. They cannot reach the heavens with their hands, to shake God's throne, else they would; but they show their ill-will by setting their mouth against the heavens. <hi type="italic">Their tongue</hi> also <hi type="italic">walks through the earth,</hi> and they take liberty to abuse all that come in their way. No man's greatness or goodness can secure him from the scourge of the virulent tongue. They take a pride and pleasure in bantering all mankind; they are pests of the country, for they neither fear God nor regard man. [4.] In all this they were very atheistical and profane. They could not have been thus wicked if they had not learned to say (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">How doth God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?</hi> So far were they from desiring the knowledge of God, who gave them all the good things they had and would have taught them to use them well, that they were not willing to believe God had any knowledge of them, that he took any notice of their wickedness or would ever call them to an account. As if, because he is <hi type="italic">Most High,</hi> he could not or would not see them, <reference osisRef="Job.22.12-Job.22.13">Job xxii. 12, 13</reference>. Whereas because he is <hi type="italic">Most High</hi> therefore he can, and will, take cognizance of all the children of men and of all they do, or say, or think. What an affront is it to the God of infinite knowledge, from whom all knowledge is, to ask, <hi type="italic">Is there knowledge in him?</hi> Well may he say (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Behold, these are the ungodly.</hi> <div eID="gen11789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11790" type="x-p"/> (3.) He observed that while wicked men thus prospered in their impiety, and were made more impious by their prosperity, good people were in great affliction, and he himself in particular, which very much strengthened the temptation he was in to quarrel with Providence. [1.] He looked abroad and saw many of God's people greatly at a loss (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.10">v. 10</reference>): "Because the wicked are so very daring <hi type="italic">therefore his people return hither;</hi> they are at the same pause, the same plunge, that I am at; they know not what to say to it any more than I do, and the rather because <hi type="italic">waters of a full cup are wrung out to them;</hi> they are not only made to drink, and to drink deeply, of the bitter cup of affliction, but to drink all. Care is taken that they lose not a drop of that unpleasant potion; the waters are wrung out unto them, that they may have the dregs of the cup. They pour out abundance of tears when they hear wicked people blaspheme God and speak profanely," as David did, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.136">Ps. cxix. 136</reference>. These are the waters wrung out to them. [2.] He looked at home, and felt himself under the continual frowns of Providence, while the wicked were sunning themselves in its smiles (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">v. 14</reference>): "For my part," says he, "<hi type="italic">all the day long have I been plagued</hi> with one affliction or another, <hi type="italic">and chastened every morning,</hi> as duly as the morning comes." His afflictions were great—he was chastened and plagued; the returns of them were constant, <hi type="italic">every morning</hi> with the morning, and they continued, without intermission, <hi type="italic">all the day long.</hi> This he thought was very hard, that, when those who blasphemed God were in prosperity, he that worshipped God was under such great affliction. He spoke feelingly when he spoke of his own troubles; there is no disputing against sense, except by faith. <div eID="gen11790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11791" type="x-p"/> (4.) From all this arose a very strong temptation to cast off his religion. [1.] Some that observed the prosperity of the wicked, especially comparing it with the afflictions of the righteous, were tempted to deny a providence and to think that God had forsaken the earth. In this sense some take <reference osisRef="Ps.73.11">v. 11</reference>. There are those, even among God's professing people, that say, "<hi type="italic">How does God know?</hi> Surely all things are left to blind fortune, and not disposed of by an all-seeing God." Some of the heathen, upon such a remark as this, have asked, <hi type="italic">Quis putet esse deos?—Who will believe that there are gods?</hi> [2.] Though the psalmist's feet were not so far gone as to question God's omniscience, yet he was tempted to question the benefit of religion, and to say (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">Verily, I have cleansed my heart in vain,</hi> and have, to no purpose, <hi type="italic">washed my hands in innocency.</hi> See here what it is to be religious; it is to cleanse our hearts, in the first place, by repentance and regeneration, and then to wash our hands in innocency by a universal reformation of our lives. It is not in vain to do this, not in vain to serve God and keep his ordinances; but good men have been sometimes tempted to say, "It is in vain," and "Religion is a thing that there is nothing to be got by," because they see wicked people in prosperity. But, however the thing may appear now, when the pure in heart, those blessed ones, shall see God (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.8">Matt. v. 8</reference>), they will not say that they cleansed their hearts in vain.
entries.e4453f82b13fd74246664bb94808bfcf9207e2aa: <div eID="gen11791" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The End of the Wicked.</title> <div sID="gen11792" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> If I say, I will speak thus; behold, I should offend <hi type="italic">against</hi> the generation of thy children. <hi type="super">16</hi> When I thought to know this, it <hi type="italic">was</hi> too painful for me; 17 Until I went into the sanctuary of God; <hi type="italic">then</hi> understood I their end. <hi type="super">18</hi> Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. <hi type="super">19</hi> How are they <hi type="italic">brought</hi> into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors. <hi type="super">20</hi> As a dream when <hi type="italic">one</hi> awaketh; <hi type="italic">so,</hi> O Lord, when thou awakest, thou shalt despise their image. <div eID="gen11792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11793" type="x-p"/> We have seen what a strong temptation the psalmist was in to envy prospering profaneness; now here we are told how he kept his footing and got the victory. <div eID="gen11793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11794" type="x-p"/> I. He kept up a respect for God's people, and with that he restrained himself from speaking what he had thought amiss, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.15">v. 15</reference>. He got the victory by degrees, and this was the first point he gained; he was ready to say, <hi type="italic">Verily, I have cleansed my heart in vain,</hi> and thought he had reason to say it, but he kept his mouth with this consideration, "<hi type="italic">If I say, I will speak thus, behold, I should</hi> myself revolt and apostatize from, and so give the greatest offence imaginable to, <hi type="italic">the generation of thy children.</hi>" Observe here, 1. Though he thought amiss, he took care not to utter that evil thought which he had conceived. Note, It is bad to think ill, but it is worse to speak it, for that is giving the evil thought an <hi type="italic">imprimatur—a sanction;</hi> it is allowing it, giving consent to it, and publishing it for the infection of others. But it is a good sign that we repent of the evil imagination of the heart if we suppress it, and the error remains with ourselves. If therefore thou hast been so foolish as to think evil, be so wise as to <hi type="italic">lay thy hand upon thy mouth,</hi> and let it go no further, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.32">Prov. xxx. 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">If I say, I will speak thus.</hi> Observe, Though his corrupt heart made this inference from the prosperity of the wicked, yet he did not mention it to those whether it were fit to be mentioned or no. Note, We must think twice before we speak once, both because some things may be thought which yet may not be spoken and because the second thoughts may correct the mistakes of the first. 2. The reason why he would not speak it was for fear of giving offence to those whom God owned for his children. Note, (1.) There are a people in the world that are the generation of God's children, a set of men that hear and love God as their Father. (2.) We must be very careful not to say or do any thing which may justly offend <hi type="italic">any of these little ones</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.6">Matt. xviii. 6</reference>), especially which may offend <hi type="italic">the generation of them,</hi> may sadden their hearts, or weaken their hands, or shake their interest. (3.) There is nothing that can give more general offence to the generation of God's children than to say that <hi type="italic">we have cleansed our heart in vain</hi> or that it is vain to serve God; for there is nothing more contrary to their universal sentiment and experience nor any thing that grieves them more than to hear God thus reflected on. (4.) Those that wish themselves in the condition of the wicked do in effect quit the tents of God's children. <div eID="gen11794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11795" type="x-p"/> II. He foresaw the ruin of wicked people. By this he baffled the temptation, as by the former he gave some check to it. Because he durst not speak what he had thought, for fear of giving offence, he began to consider whether he had any good reason for that thought (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">v. 16</reference>): "I endeavoured to understand the meaning of this unaccountable dispensation of Providence; but <hi type="italic">it was too painful for me.</hi> I could not conquer it by the strength of my own reasoning." It is a problem, not to be solved by the mere light of nature, for, if there were not another life after this, we could not fully reconcile the prosperity of the wicked with the justice of God. But (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">v. 17</reference>) <hi type="italic">he went into the sanctuary of God;</hi> he applied to his devotions, meditated upon the attributes of God, and the <hi type="italic">things revealed, which belong to us and to our children;</hi> he consulted the scriptures, and the lips of the priests who attended the sanctuary; he prayed to God to make this matter plain to him and to help him over this difficulty; and, at length, he understood the wretched end of wicked people, which he plainly foresaw to be such that even in the height of their prosperity they were rather to be pitied than envied, for they were but ripening for ruin. Note, There are many great things, and things needful to be known, which will not be known otherwise than by going into the sanctuary of God, by the word and prayer. The sanctuary must therefore be the resort of a tempted soul. Note, further, We must judge of persons and things as they appear by the light of divine revelation, and then we shall judge righteous judgment; particularly we must judge by the end. All is well that ends well, everlastingly well; but nothing well that ends ill, everlastingly ill. The righteous man's afflictions end in peace, and therefore he is happy; the wicked man's enjoyments end in destruction, and therefore he is miserable. <div eID="gen11795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11796" type="x-p"/> 1. The prosperity of the wicked is short and uncertain. The high places in which Providence sets them are <hi type="italic">slippery places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.18">v. 18</reference>), where they cannot long keep footing; but, when they offer to climb higher, that very attempt will be the occasion of their sliding and falling. Their prosperity has no firm ground; it is not built upon God's favour or his promise; and they have not the satisfaction of feeling that it rests on firm ground. <div eID="gen11796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11797" type="x-p"/> 2. Their destruction is sure, and sudden, and very great. This cannot be meant of any temporal destruction; for they were supposed to <hi type="italic">spend all their days in wealth</hi> and their death itself had no bands in it: <hi type="italic">In a moment they go down to the grace,</hi> so that even that could scarcely be called <hi type="italic">their destruction;</hi> it must therefore be meant of eternal destruction on the other side death—hell and destruction. They flourish for a time, but are undone for ever. (1.) Their ruin is sure and inevitable. He speaks of it as a thing done—<hi type="italic">They are cast down;</hi> for their destruction is as certain as if it were already accomplished. He speaks of it as God's doing, and therefore it cannot be resisted: <hi type="italic">Thou castest them down.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">destruction from the Almighty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.15">Joel i. 15</reference>), from <hi type="italic">the glory of his power,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.9">2 Thess. i. 9</reference>. Who can support those whom God will cast down, on whom God will lay burdens? (2.) It is swift and sudden; their damnation slumbers not; for <hi type="italic">how are they brought into desolation as in a moment!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.19">v. 19</reference>. It is easily effected, and will be a great surprise to themselves and all about them. (3.) It is severe and very dreadful. It is a total and final ruin: <hi type="italic">They are utterly consumed with terrors,</hi> It is the misery of the damned that the terrors of the Almighty, whom they have made their enemy, fasten upon their guilty consciences, which can neither shelter themselves from them nor strengthen themselves under them; and therefore not their being, but their bliss, must needs be utterly consumed by them; not the least degree of comfort or hope remains to them; the higher they were lifted up in their prosperity the sorer will their fall be when they are cast down into <hi type="italic">destructions</hi> (for the word is plural) and suddenly <hi type="italic">brought into desolation.</hi> <div eID="gen11797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11798" type="x-p"/> 3. Their prosperity is therefore not to be envied at all, but despised rather, <hi type="italic">quod erat demonstrandum—which was the point to be established,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.20">v. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">As a dream when one awaketh, so, O Lord! when thou awakest,</hi> or when they awake (as some read it), <hi type="italic">thou shalt despise their image,</hi> their shadow, <hi type="italic">and make it to vanish. In the day of the great judgment</hi> (so the Chaldee paraphrase reads it), when they are awaked out of their graves, thou shalt, in wrath, despise their image; for <hi type="italic">they shall rise to shame and everlasting contempt.</hi> See here, (1.) What their prosperity now is; it is but an image, a vain show, a fashion of the world that passes away; it is not real, but imaginary, and it is only a corrupt imagination that makes it a happiness; it is not substance, but a mere shadow; it is not what it seems to be, nor will it prove what we promise ourselves from it; it is as a dream, which may please us a little, while we are asleep, yet even then it disturbs our repose; but, how pleasing soever it is, it is all but a cheat, all false; when we awake we find it so. A hungry man <hi type="italic">dreams that he eats, but he awakes and his soul is empty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">Isa. xxix. 8</reference>. A man is never the more rich or honourable for dreaming he is so. Who therefore will envy a man the pleasure of a dream? (2.) What will be the issue of it; God will awake to judgment, to plead his own and his people's injured cause; they shall be made to awake out of the sleep of their carnal security, and then God shall despise their image; he shall make it appear to all the world how despicable it is; so that the righteous shall laugh at them, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.6-Ps.52.7">Ps. lii. 6, 7</reference>. How did God despise that rich man's image when he said, <hi type="italic">Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee!</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19-Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 19, 20</reference>. We ought to be of God's mind, for his judgment is according to truth, and not to admire and envy that which he despises and will despise; for, sooner or later, he will bring all the world to be of his mind.
entries.199315cbdc7aee03d819f971f40ca81649183d59: <div eID="gen11798" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Devout Confidence.</title> <div sID="gen11799" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Thus my heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins. <hi type="super">22</hi> So foolish <hi type="italic">was</hi> I, and ignorant: I was <hi type="italic">as</hi> a beast before thee. <hi type="super">23</hi> Nevertheless I <hi type="italic">am</hi> continually with thee: thou hast holden <hi type="italic">me</hi> by my right hand. 24 Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me <hi type="italic">to</hi> glory. <hi type="super">25</hi> Whom have I in heaven <hi type="italic">but thee?</hi> and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none upon earth <hi type="italic">that</hi> I desire beside thee. <hi type="super">26</hi> My flesh and my heart faileth: <hi type="italic">but</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever. 27 For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish: thou hast destroyed all them that go a whoring from thee. <hi type="super">28</hi> But <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , that I may declare all thy works. <div eID="gen11799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11800" type="x-p"/> Behold Samson's riddle again unriddled, <hi type="italic">Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong sweetness;</hi> for we have here an account of the good improvement which the psalmist made of that sore temptation with which he had been assaulted and by which he was almost overcome. He that stumbles and does not fall, by recovering himself takes so much the longer steps forward. It was so with the psalmist here; many good lessons he learned from his temptation, his struggles with it, and his victories over it. Nor would God suffer his people to be tempted if his grace were not sufficient for them, not only to save them from harm, but to make them gainers by it; even this shall work for good. <div eID="gen11800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11801" type="x-p"/> I. He learned to think very humbly of himself and to abase and accuse himself before God (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.21-Ps.73.22">v. 21, 22</reference>); he reflects with shame upon the disorder and danger he was in, and the vexation he gave himself by entertaining the temptation and parleying with it: <hi type="italic">My heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins,</hi> as one afflicted with the acute pain of the stone in the region of the kidneys. If evil thoughts at any time enter into the mind of a good man, he does not roll them under his tongue as a sweet morsel, but they are grievous and painful to him; temptation was to Paul as a thorn in the flesh, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2 Cor. xii. 7</reference>. This particular temptation, the working of envy and discontent, is as painful as any; where it constantly rests it is the <hi type="italic">rottenness of the bones</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.30">Prov. xiv. 30</reference>); where it does but occasionally come it is the pricking of the reins. Fretfulness is a corruption that is its own correction. Now in the reflection upon it, 1. He owns it was his folly thus to vex himself: "<hi type="italic">So foolish was I</hi> to be my own tormentor." Let peevish people thus reproach themselves for, and shame themselves out of, their discontents. "What a fool am I thus to make myself uneasy without a cause?" 2. He owns it was his ignorance to vex himself at this: "So ignorant was I of that which I might have known, and which, if I had known it aright, would have been sufficient to silence my murmurs. <hi type="italic">I was as a beast (Behemoth—a great beast) before thee.</hi> Beasts mind present things only, and never look before at what is to come; and so did I. If I had not been a great fool, I should never have suffered such a senseless temptation to prevail over me so far. What! to envy wicked men upon account of their prosperity! To be ready to wish myself one of them, and to think of changing conditions with them! <hi type="italic">So foolish was I.</hi>" Note, If good men do at any time, through the surprise and strength of temptation, think, or speak, or act amiss, when they see their error they will reflect upon it with sorrow, and shame, and self-abhorrence, will call themselves <hi type="italic">fools</hi> for it. <hi type="italic">Surely I am more brutish than any man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.2">Prov. xxx. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.5-Job.42.6">Job xlii. 5, 6</reference>. Thus David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.10">2 Sam. xxiv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen11801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11802" type="x-p"/> II. He took occasion hence to own his dependence on and obligations to the grace of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.23">v. 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Nevertheless,</hi> foolish as I am, <hi type="italic">I am continually with thee</hi> and in thy favour; <hi type="italic">thou hast holden me by my right hand.</hi>" This may refer either, 1. To the care God had taken of him, and the kindness he had shown him, all along from his beginning hitherto. He had said, in the hour of temptation (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">All the day long have I been plagued;</hi> but here he corrects himself for that passionate complaint: "Though God has chastened me, he has not cast me off; notwithstanding all the crosses of my life, <hi type="italic">I have been continually with thee;</hi> I have had thy presence with me, and thou hast been nigh unto me in all that which I have called upon thee for; and therefore, though perplexed, yet not in despair. Though God has sometimes written bitter things against me, yet he has still <hi type="italic">holden me by my right hand,</hi> both to keep me, that I should not desert him or fly off from him, and to prevent my sinking and fainting under my burdens, or losing my way in the wildernesses through which I have walked." If we have been kept in the way with God, kept closely in our duty and upheld in our integrity, we must own ourselves indebted to the free grace of God for our preservation: <hi type="italic">Having obtained help of God, I continue hitherto.</hi> And, if he has thus maintained the spiritual life, the earnest of eternal life, we ought not to complain, whatever calamities of this present time we have met with. Or, 2. To the late experience he had had of the power of divine grace in carrying him through this strong temptation and bringing him off a conqueror: "I was foolish and ignorant, and yet thou hast had compassion on me and taught me (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.2">Heb. v. 2</reference>), and kept me under thy protection;" for the unworthiness of man is no bar to the free grace of God. We must ascribe our safety in temptation, and our victory over it, not to our own wisdom, for we are foolish and ignorant, but to the gracious presence of God with us and the prevalency of Christ's intercession for us, that our faith may not fail: "<hi type="italic">My feet were almost gone,</hi> and they would have quite gone, past recovery, but that thou hast holden me by my right hand and so kept me from falling." <div eID="gen11802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11803" type="x-p"/> III. He encouraged himself to hope that the same God who had delivered him from this evil work would <hi type="italic">preserve him to his heavenly kingdom,</hi> as St. Paul does (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 18</reference>): "I am now upheld by thee, therefore <hi type="italic">thou shalt guide me with thy counsel,</hi> leading me, as thou hast done hitherto, many a difficult step; and, since I am now continually with thee, thou <hi type="italic">shalt afterwards receive me to glory</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.73.24">v. 24</reference>. This completes the happiness of the saints, so that they have no reason to envy the worldly prosperity of sinners. Note, 1. All those who commit themselves to God shall be guided with his counsel, with the counsel both of his word and of his Spirit, the best counsellors. The psalmist had like to have paid dearly for following his own counsels in this temptation and therefore resolves for the future to take God's advice, which shall never be wanting to those that duly seek it with a resolution to follow it. 2. All those who are guided and led by the counsel of God in this world shall be received to his glory in another world. If we make God's glory in us the end we aim at, he will make our glory with him the end we shall for ever be happy in. Upon this consideration, let us never envy sinners, but rather bless ourselves in our own blessedness. If God direct us in the way of our duty, and prevent our turning aside out of it, he will afterwards, when our state of trial and preparation is over, receive us to his kingdom and glory, the believing hopes and prospects of which will reconcile us to all the dark providences that now puzzle and perplex us, and ease us of the pain we have been put into by some threatening temptations. <div eID="gen11803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11804" type="x-p"/> IV. He was hereby quickened to cleave the more closely to God, and very much confirmed and comforted in the choice he had made of him, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.25-Ps.73.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. His thoughts here dwell with delight upon his own happiness in God, as much greater then the happiness of the ungodly that prospered in the world. He saw little reason to envy them what they had in the creature when he found how much more and better, surer and sweeter, comforts he had in the Creator, and what cause he had to congratulate himself on this account. He had complained of his afflictions (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">v. 14</reference>); but this makes them very light and easy, <hi type="italic">All is well if God be mine.</hi> We have here the breathings of a sanctified soul towards God, and its repose in him, as that to a godly man really which the prosperity of a worldly man is to him in conceit and imagination: <hi type="italic">Whom have I in heaven but thee?</hi> There is scarcely a verse in all the psalms more expressive than this of the pious and devout affections of a soul to God; here it soars up towards him, follows hard after him, and yet, at the same time, has an entire satisfaction and complacency in him. <div eID="gen11804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11805" type="x-p"/> 1. It is here supposed that God alone is the felicity and chief good of man. He, and he only, that made the soul, can make it happy; there is none in heaven, none in earth, that can pretend to do it besides. <div eID="gen11805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11806" type="x-p"/> 2. Here are expressed the workings and breathings of a soul towards God accordingly. If God be our felicity, <div eID="gen11806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11807" type="x-p"/> (1.) Then we must have him (<hi type="italic">Whom have I but thee?</hi>), we must choose him, and make sure to ourselves an interest in him. What will it avail us that he is the felicity of souls if he be not the felicity of our souls, and if we do not by a lively faith make him ours, by joining ourselves to him in an everlasting covenant? <div eID="gen11807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11808" type="x-p"/> (2.) Then our desire must be towards him and our delight in him (the word signifies both); we must delight in what we have of God and desire what we yet further hope for. Our desires must not only be offered up to God, but they must all terminate in him, desiring nothing more than God, but still more and more of him. This includes all our prayers, <hi type="italic">Lord, give us thyself;</hi> as that includes all the promises, <hi type="italic">I will be to them a God. The desire of our souls is to thy name.</hi> <div eID="gen11808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11809" type="x-p"/> (3.) We must prefer him in our choice and desire before any other. [1.] "<hi type="italic">There is none in heaven but thee,</hi> none to seek to or trust in, none to court or covet acquaintance with, but thee." God is in himself more glorious than any celestial being (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.6">Ps. lxxxix. 6</reference>), and must be, in our eyes, infinitely more desirable. Excellent beings there are in heaven, but God alone can make us happy. His favour is infinitely more to us than the refreshment of the dews of heaven or the benign influence of the stars of heaven, more than the friendship of the saints in heaven or the good offices of the angels there. [2.] <hi type="italic">I desire none on earth besides thee;</hi> not only none in heaven, a place at a distance, which we have but little acquaintance with, but none on earth neither, where we have many friends and where much of our present interest and concern lie. "Earth carries away the desires of most men, and yet I have none on earth, no persons, no things, no possessions, no delights, that I desire besides thee or with thee, in comparison or competition with thee." We must desire nothing besides God but what we desire for him (<hi type="italic">nil præter te nisi propter te—nothing besides thee except for thy sake</hi>), nothing but what we desire from him, and can be content without so that it be made up in him. We must desire nothing besides God as needful to be a partner with him in making us happy. <div eID="gen11809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11810" type="x-p"/> (4.) Then we must repose ourselves in God with an entire satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.26">v. 26</reference>. Observe here, [1.] Great distress and trouble supposed: <hi type="italic">My flesh and my heart fail.</hi> Note, Others have experienced and we must expect, the failing both of flesh and heart. The body will fail by sickness, age, and death; and that which touches the bone and the flesh touches us in a tender part, that part of ourselves which we have been but too fond of; when the flesh fails the heart is ready to fail too; the conduct, courage, and comfort fail. [2.] Sovereign relief provided in this distress: <hi type="italic">But God is the strength of my heart and my portion for ever.</hi> Note, Gracious souls, in their greatest distresses, rest upon God as their spiritual strength and their eternal portion. <hi type="italic">First, "He is the strength of my heart,</hi> the rock of my heart, a firm foundation, which will bear my weight and not sink under it. <hi type="italic">God is the strength of my heart;</hi> I have found him so; I do so still, and hope ever to find him so." In the distress supposed, he had put the case of a double failure, both <hi type="italic">flesh and heart fail;</hi> but, in the relief, he fastens on a single support: he leaves out the flesh and the consideration of that, it is enough that God is <hi type="italic">the strength of his heart.</hi> He speaks as one careless of the body (let that fail, there is no remedy), but as one concerned about the soul, to be <hi type="italic">strengthened in the inner man.</hi> Secondly, <hi type="italic">"He is my portion for ever;</hi> he will not only support me while I am here, but make me happy when I go hence." The saints choose God for their portion, they have him for their portion, and it is their happiness that he will be their portion, a portion that will last as long as the immortal soul lasts. <div eID="gen11810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11811" type="x-p"/> V. He was fully convinced of the miserable condition of all wicked people. This he learned in the sanctuary upon this occasion, and he would never forget it (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lo, those that are far from thee,</hi> in a state of distance and estrangement, that desire the Almighty to depart from them, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> certainly <hi type="italic">perish;</hi> so shall their doom be; they choose to be far from God, and they shall be far from him for ever. <hi type="italic">Thou wilt</hi> justly <hi type="italic">destroy all those that go a whoring from thee,</hi> that is, all apostates, that in profession have been betrothed to God, but forsake him, their duty to him and their communion with him, to embrace the bosom of a stranger." The doom is sever, no less than perishing and being destroyed. It is universal: "They shall all be destroyed without exception." It is certain: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast destroyed;</hi> it is as sure to be done as if done already; and the destruction of some ungodly men is an earnest of the perdition of all." God himself undertakes to do it, into whose hands it is a fearful thing to fall: "Thou, though infinite in goodness, wilt reckon for thy injured honour and abused patience, and wilt destroy those that go a whoring from thee." <div eID="gen11811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11812" type="x-p"/> VI. He was greatly encouraged to cleave to God and to confide in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.28">v. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">If those that are far from God shall perish,</hi> then, 1. Let this constrain us to live in communion with God; "if it fare so ill with those that live at a distance from him, then it is good, very good, the chief good, that good for a man, in this life, which he should most carefully pursue and secure, it is best for me to draw near to God, and to have God draw near to me;" the original may take in both. <hi type="italic">But for my part</hi> (so I would read it) <hi type="italic">the approach of God is good for me.</hi> Our drawing near to God takes rise from his drawing near to us, and it is the happy meeting that makes the bliss. Here is a great truth laid down, That it is good to draw near to God; but the life of it lies in the application, "It is good for <hi type="italic">me.</hi>" Those are the wise who know what is good for themselves: "<hi type="italic">It is good,</hi> says he (and every good man agrees with him in it), <hi type="italic">it is good for me to draw near to God;</hi> it is my duty; it is my interest." 2. Let us therefore live in a continual dependence upon him: "<hi type="italic">I have put my trust in the Lord God,</hi> and will never go a whoring from him after any creature confidences." If wicked men, notwithstanding all their prosperity, shall perish and be destroyed, then let us trust in the Lord God, in him, not in them (see <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3-Ps.146.5">Ps. cxlvi. 3-5</reference>), in him, and not in our worldly prosperity; let us trust in God, and neither fret at them nor be afraid of them; let us trust in him for a better portion than theirs is. 3. While we do so, let us not doubt but that we shall have occasion to praise his name. Let us trust in the Lord, that we may declare all his works. Note, Those that with an upright heart put their trust in God shall never want matter for thanksgiving to him.  <chapter eID="Ps.73"/> <div eID="gen11812" type="x-p"/>

entries.89e4949cea2a991da5b7c84420a68ead91456a05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6304"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 73</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.73.1-Ps.73.28">Psa 73:1-28</reference>. Of Asaph--(see Introduction). God is good to His people. For although the prosperity of the wicked, and the afflictions of the righteous, tempted the Psalmist to misgivings of God's government, yet the sudden and fearful ruin of the ungodly, seen in the light of God's revelation, reassures his heart; and, chiding himself for his folly, he is led to confide renewedly in God, and celebrate His goodness and love.</title> <div sID="gen9656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6304"/>1. The abrupt announcement of the theme indicates that it is the conclusion of a perplexing mental conflict, which is then detailed (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.4">Jr 12:1-4</reference>).<div eID="gen9656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Truly--</hi>or, "Surely it is so."<div eID="gen9657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clean heart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Psa 18:26</reference>) describes the true Israel. <div eID="gen9658" type="x-p"/>
entries.623661845584ec74fec2ec6f39521d2907262f33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6305"/><div sID="gen9659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6305"/>2. The figures express his wavering faith, by terms denoting tottering and weakness (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.5">Psa 22:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">62:3</reference>). <div eID="gen9659" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac0e99d9141b8a95dc29307eeaf5f34cf218afd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6306"/><div sID="gen9660" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6306"/> <hi type="bold">3-9. The prosperous wicked are insolently proud (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.5">Psa 5:5</reference>). They die, as well as live, free from perplexities: pride adorns them, and violence is their clothing; indeed they are inflated with unexpected success. With all this--</hi>  <div eID="gen9660" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbcc3448f9a7e69b731434396688139d8b970eed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6308"/><div sID="gen9662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6308"/>10-12. Hence God's people are confounded, turned hither (or back) and thither, perplexed with doubts of God's knowledge and care, and filled with sorrow. <div eID="gen9662" type="x-p"/>
entries.5168417accc7019f1e73c65b6fc9659acc8a0618: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6310"/><div sID="gen9664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6310"/>13-14. The Psalmist, partaking of these troubles, is especially disturbed in view of his own case, that with all his diligent efforts for a holy life, he is still sorely tried. <div eID="gen9664" type="x-p"/>
entries.51aee0302509ec8b45a3485ba13cb73a7d947841: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6311"/><div sID="gen9665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6311"/>15. Freed from idiomatic phrases, this verse expresses a supposition, as, "Had I thus spoken, I should," &c., intimating that he had kept his troubles to himself.<div eID="gen9665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">generation of thy children--</hi>Thy people (<reference osisRef="1John.3.1">1Jo 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen9666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9667" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offend--</hi>literally, "deceive, mislead." <div eID="gen9667" type="x-p"/>
entries.57db76ddad05f513fb2ba6637e4bc73b3494b7cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6312"/><div sID="gen9668" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6312"/> <hi type="bold">16-17. Still he--</hi> <div eID="gen9668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thought--</hi>literally, "studied," or, "pondered this riddle"; but in vain; it remained a toil (compare Margin), till he-- <div eID="gen9669" type="x-p"/>
entries.9dc99548921b3b0de57340d17a428924d77f4530: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6314"/><div sID="gen9671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6314"/><hi type="bold">18-20. their end--</hi>future (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">Psa 37:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.38">38</reference>), which is dismal and terribly sudden (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.27">Pr 1:27</reference>; 29:1), aggravated and hastened by terror. As one despises an unsubstantial dream, so God, waking up to judgment (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Psa 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">44:23</reference>), despises their vain shadow of happiness (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">Psa 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">Is 29:7</reference>). They are thrown into ruins as a building falling to pieces (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.3">Psa 74:3</reference>). <div eID="gen9671" type="x-p"/>
entries.610f525c7de6b74eff5d6fdd7943eb52b40c07c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6315"/><div sID="gen9672" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6315"/> <hi type="bold">21-22. He confesses how--</hi> <div eID="gen9672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foolish--</hi>literally, "stupid," and<div eID="gen9673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ignorant--</hi>literally, "not discerning," had been his course of thought. <div eID="gen9674" type="x-p"/>
entries.86059701e3216d8845ab94048022ff50692db16a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6317"/><div sID="gen9676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6317"/>23. Still he was with God, as a dependent beneficiary, and so kept from falling (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Psa 73:2</reference>). <div eID="gen9676" type="x-p"/>

All doubts are silenced in confidence of divine guidance and future glory.<div eID="gen9677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receive me to glory--</hi>literally, "take for (me) glory" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Psa 68:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ep 4:8</reference>). <div eID="gen9678" type="x-p"/>

entries.2d410f06e1fced0b2791c4a5a19b0c14b3fb07ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6321"/><div sID="gen9682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6321"/>27-28. The lot of apostates, described by a figure of frequent use (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">Jr 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.35">Eze 23:35</reference>), is contrasted with his, who finds happiness in nearness to God (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.8">Jas 4:8</reference>), and his delightful work the declaration of His praise. <chapter eID="Ps.73"/>

entries.56f18db57ca2a30d01903115c975d8fd23a7dc81: <div eID="gen20947" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20948" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20949" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20949" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20948" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20950" type="x-p"/> The psalmist speaks of God's goodness to his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.73.1">Psa 73:1</reference>; shows how much he was stumbled at the prosperity of the wicked, and describes their state, <reference osisRef="Psa.73.2-Psa.73.12">Psa 73:2-12</reference>; details the process of the temptation, and the pain he suffered in consequence, <reference osisRef="Psa.73.13-Psa.73.16">Psa 73:13-16</reference>; shows how he was delivered, and the dismal reverse of the state of the once prosperous ungodly man, by which his own false views were corrected, <reference osisRef="Psa.73.17-Psa.73.22">Psa 73:17-22</reference>; his great confidence in God, and the good consequences of it, <reference osisRef="Psa.73.23-Psa.73.28">Psa 73:23-28</reference>. <div eID="gen20950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20951" type="x-p"/> This is the commencement of the Third Book of the Psalter; and the Psalm before us has for title, A Psalm of Asaph; or, as the margin has it, A Psalm for Asaph. The title in the Hebrew is מזמור לאסף mizmor leasaph; "A Psalm of Asaph:" and it is likely that this Asaph was the composer of it; that he lived under the Babylonish captivity; and that he published this Psalm to console the Israelites under bondage, who were greatly tried to find themselves in such outward distress and misery, while a people much more wicked and corrupt than they, were in great prosperity, and held them in bondage. <div eID="gen20951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20952" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20953" type="x-p"/> Truly God is good to Israel - Captives as they were, they still had many blessings from God; and they had promises of deliverance, which must be fulfilled in due time. <div eID="gen20953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20954" type="x-p"/> Such as are of a clean heart - Those who have a clean heart must have inward happiness: and, because they resemble God, they can never be forsaken by him.
entries.486fb0d451af478768a9fa105583137c1dc36680: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20955" type="x-p"/> My feet were almost gone - I had nearly given up my confidence. I was ready to find fault with the dispensations of providence; and thought the Judge of all the earth did not do right.
entries.b5dbce57f20aa6308023cd0c0fca8803f3974af5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20956" type="x-p"/> I was envious at the foolish - I saw persons who worshipped not the true God, and others who were abandoned to all vices, in possession of every temporal comfort, while the godly were in straits, difficulties, and affliction. I began then to doubt whether there was a wise providence; and my mind became irritated. It seems to have been a maxim among the ancient heathens, Θεου ονειδος τους κακους ευδαιμονειν, "The prosperity of the wicked is a reproach to the gods." But they had no just conception of a state of future rewards and punishments. Besides, man could not bear prosperity. If men had uninterrupted comforts here, perhaps not one soul would ever seek a preparation for heaven. Human trials and afflictions, the general warfare of human life, are the highest proof of a providence as benevolent as it is wise. Were the state of human affairs different from what it is, hell would be more thickly peopled; and there would be fewer inhabitants in glory. There is reason to doubt whether there would be any religion upon earth had we nothing but temporal prosperity. Indeed, all the following verses are proofs of it.
entries.7b562178ee1020010d09cf79820b7857cb2c345f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20957" type="x-p"/> No bands in their death - Many of the godly have sore conflicts at their death. Their enemy then thrusts sore at them that they may fall; or that their confidence in their God may be shaken. But of this the ungodly know nothing. Satan will not molest them; he is sure of his prey; they are entangled, and cannot now break their nets; their consciences are seared, they have no sense of guilt. If they think at all of another world, they presume on that mercy which they never sought, and of which they have no distinct notion. Perhaps, "they die without a sigh or a groan; and thus go off as quiet as a lamb" - to the slaughter.
entries.6afb284c27e0af714c3d991a773cbe13daf90438: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20958" type="x-p"/> Pride compasseth them about as a chain - Perhaps there is an allusion here to the office which some of them bore. Chains of gold, and golden rings, were ensigns of magistracy and civil power. As these chains encompassed their necks, or the rings their wrists and fingers, as the signs of the offices in virtue of which they acted; so חמס chamas, violence, oppressive conduct, encompassed them. They made no other use of their great power, than to oppress the poor and the needy; and to drive things to extremities. The Chaldee, instead of a chain, represents this as a crown or diadem, which they had formed out of the plunder of the poor and defenseless.
entries.7c5a80dc219b1f4f2eda86ef9645049d2d36ab25: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20959" type="x-p"/> Their eyes stand out with fatness - "Their countenance is changed because of fatness." - Chaldee. By fatness, or corpulency, the natural lines of the face are changed, or rather obliterated. The characteristic distinctions are gone; and we see little remaining besides the human hog. <div eID="gen20959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20960" type="x-p"/> They have more than heart could wish - I doubt this translation. Whose heart ever said, I have enough, which had not its portion with God? It would be more literal to say, "They surpass the thoughts of their heart." They have more than they expected, though not more than they wish.
entries.8f509ffeaa97baed9ea810038567cd8db018c93e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20961" type="x-p"/> They are corrupt - ימיקו yamiku, they mock, act dissolutely. <div eID="gen20961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20962" type="x-p"/> And speak wickedly concerning oppression - They vindicate excessive acts of government: they push justice to its rigour. They neither show equity, lenity, nor mercy; they are cruel, and they vindicate their proceedings.
entries.1c4b3e22415168efd6bc855ba6efffc623488a1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20963" type="x-p"/> Set their mouth against the heavens - They blaspheme God, ridicule religion, mock at Providence, and laugh at a future state. <div eID="gen20963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20964" type="x-p"/> Their tongue walketh through the earth - They find fault with every thing; they traduce the memory of the just in heaven, and ridicule the saints that are upon earth. They criticize every dispensation of God.
entries.68c32e2a00b1e9cc29b38e3ce47834c5a413c7d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20965" type="x-p"/> Therefore his people return hither - There are very few verses in the Bible that have been more variously translated than this; and, like the man in the fable, they have blown the hot to cool it, and the cold to warm it. It has been translated, "Therefore God's people fall off to them; and thence they reap no small advantage." And, "Therefore let his people come before them; and waters in full measure would be wrung out from them." That is, "Should God's people come before them, they would squeeze them to the utmost; they would wring out all the juice in their bodies." The Chaldee has, "Therefore, are they turned against the people of the Lord, that they may bruise and beat them with mallets; that they may pour out to them abundance of tears." The Vulgate, "Therefore shall my people return here, and days of abundance shall be found by them." The Septuagint is the same. The Ethiopic, Arabic, and Syriac, nearly the same. The Hebrew text is, לכן ישוב עמו הלם ומי מלא ימצו למו lachen yashub ammo (עמי ammi) halom; umey male yimmatsu lamo; "Therefore shall my people be converted, where they shall find abundance of waters." That is, The people, seeing the iniquity of the Babylonians, and feeling their oppressive hand, shall be converted to me; and I shall bring them to their own land, where they shall find an abundance of all the necessaries of life. I believe this to be the meaning; and thus we find their afflictions were sanctified to them; for they obliged them to return to God, and then God caused them to return to their own land. The Vulgate translates ומי מלא umey male, "abundance of waters," by et dies pleni, "and days of plenty;" for it has read ימי yemey, days, for ומי umey, and waters. Almost all the Versions support this reading; but it is not acknowledged by any MS. The old Psalter is here mutilated.
entries.4fbe9732993e367f9d6c0816861ecdd001eab2c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20966" type="x-p"/> They say, How doth God know? - My people are so stumbled with the prosperity of the wicked, that they are ready in their temptation to say, "Surely, God cannot know these things, or he would never dispense his favors thus." Others consider these words as the saying of the wicked: "We may oppress these people as we please, and live as we list; God knows nothing about it."
entries.23d1393dc73cd32f4ba3938a369a97395a59c38f: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20967" type="x-p"/> These are the ungodly - The people still speak. It is the ungodly that prosper, the irreligious and profane.
entries.426ac1178bf96780aae0622d8f2846e7527df83d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen20967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20968" type="x-p"/> I have cleansed my heart in vain - It is no advantage to us to worship the true God, to walk according to the law of righteousness, and keep the ordinances of the Most High.
entries.6ee5074db97b04a6f28ac24edec167d1ceb8a03e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20969" type="x-p"/> For all the day long have I been plagued - Far from enjoying worldly prosperity, we are not only poor, but we are afflicted also; and every succeeding day brings with it some new trouble.
entries.ba40e878518bd38a67d7701e2491a4807d313c4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen20969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20970" type="x-p"/> If I say, I will speak thus - I have at last discovered that I have reasoned incorrectly; and that I have the uniform testimony of all thy children against me. From generation to generation they have testified that the Judge of all the earth does right; they have trusted in thee, and were never confounded. They also met with afflictions and sore trials, but thou didst bring them safely through all, didst sustain them in the worst, and sanctifiedst the whole to their eternal good.
entries.cb2d0706dff69e7387ca2bf7215ee1e375f4da13: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20971" type="x-p"/> When I thought to know this - When I reviewed the history of our fathers, I saw that, though thou hadst from time to time hidden thy face because of their sins, yet thou hadst never utterly abandoned them to their adversaries; and it was not reasonable to conclude that thou wouldst do now what thou hadst never done before; and yet the continuance of our captivity, the oppressive hardships which we suffer, and the small prospect there is of release, puzzle me again. These things have been very painful to me.
entries.fedcb05677d476fbcd71f79e829f1bfbbec087a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20972" type="x-p"/> Until I went into the sanctuary - Until, in the use of thy ordinances, I entered into a deep consideration of thy secret counsels, and considered the future state of the righteous and the wicked; that the unequal distribution of temporal good and evil argued a future judgment; that the present is a state of trial; and that God exercises his followers according to his godly wisdom and tender mercy. Then light sprang up in my mind, and I was assured that all these exercises were for our benefit, and that the prosperity of the wicked here was a prelude to their destruction. And this I saw to be their end. <div eID="gen20972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20973" type="x-p"/> That this Psalm was written during the captivity, there is little room to doubt. How then can the psalmist speak of the sanctuary? There was none at Babylon; and at Jerusalem it had been long since destroyed? There is no way to solve this difficulty but by considering that מקדשי mikdeshey may be taken in the sense of holy places - places set apart for prayer and meditation. And that the captives had such places in them captivity, there can be no doubt; and the place that is set apart to meet God in, for prayer, supplication, confession of sin, and meditation, is holy unto the Lord; and is, therefore, his sanctuary, whether a house or the open field. Calmet thinks by holy meditations a view of the Divine secrets, to which he refers, <reference osisRef="Psa.73.24">Psa 73:24</reference>, is here meant.
entries.b55f0e4261f0455c4a9c3827e8865e784c13d727: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20974" type="x-p"/> Thou didst set them on slippery places - Affluence is a slippery path; few have ever walked in it without falling. It is possible to be faithful in the unrighteous mammon, but it is very difficult. No man should desire riches; for they bring with them so many cares and temptations as to be almost unmanageabe. Rich men, even when pious, are seldom happy; they do not enjoy the consolations of religion. A good man, possessed of very extensive estates, unblamable in his whole deportment, once said to me: "There must be some strange malignity in riches thus to keep me in continual bondage, and deprive me of the consolations of the Gospel." Perhaps to a person to whom his estates are a snare, the words of our Lord may be literally applicable: "Sell what thou hast, and give to the poor; and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up thy cross, and follow me." But he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions! May we not then say with the psalmist, Surely thou digest set them in slippery places, etc.?
entries.789f27039d10b4c7f34bdcfa5fe09508abe4986e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20975" type="x-p"/> Are they brought into desolation - This is often a literal fact. I have known several cases where persons, very rich, have by sudden losses been brought into desolation as in a moment; in consequence of which they were utterly consumed in terrors.
entries.927fdc4d5d52e350be8c626881ea83e83524e05f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen20975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20976" type="x-p"/> As a dream when one awaketh - So their goods fled away. Their possession was a dream - their privation, real. <div eID="gen20976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20977" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt despise their image - While destitute of true religion, whatever appearance they had of greatness, nobility, honor, and happiness; yet in the sight of God they had no more than the ghost or shade of excellence which God is said here to despise. Who would be rich at such risk and dishonor?
entries.89fcbb2b1a99a4afc98a2029c1cc745edfb790cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen20977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20978" type="x-p"/> Thus may heart was grieved - The different views which I got of this subject quite confounded me; I was equally astonished at their sudden overthrow and my own ignorance. I felt as if I were a beast in stupidity. I permitted my mind to be wholly occupied with sensible things, like the beasts that perish and did not look into a future state; nor did I consider, nor submit to, the wise designs of an unerring Providence.
entries.efbeae2f6b101404ce7744d8cd26f100d7efefce: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen20978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20979" type="x-p"/> I am continually with thee - I now see that myself and my people are under thy guardian care; that we are continually upheld by thee; and while in thy right hand, we shall not be utterly cast down.
entries.d89702e3324e767a4f77556970d244a63c0e10b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen20979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20980" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel - After we have suffered awhile, receiving directions and consolations from thy good Spirit, by means of thy prophets, who are in the same captivity with ourselves; thou wilt grant us deliverance, restore us to our own land, and crown us with honor and happiness. Any sincere follower of God may use these words in reference to this and the coming world. Thy counsel - thy Word and Spirit, shall guide me through life; and when I have done and suffered thy righteous will, thou wilt receive me into thy eternal glory.
entries.a8c18fd8c7a6617c88205f17a4ca1cffaae3451c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen20980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20981" type="x-p"/> Whom have I in heaven but thee? - The original is more emphatic: מי לי בשמים ועמך לא חפצתי בארץ mi li bashshamayim; veimmecha lo chaphatsti baarets. "Who is there to me in the heavens? And with thee I have desired nothing in the earth." No man can say this who has not taken God for his portion in reference to both worlds.
entries.b2f6ef0c345040f273573574fe30c4c35a792505: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen20981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20982" type="x-p"/> My flesh - faileth - I shall soon die: and my heart - even my natural courage, will fail; and no support but what is supernatural will then be available. Therefore, he adds: <div eID="gen20982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20983" type="x-p"/> God is the strength of my heart - Literally, the rock of my heart. <div eID="gen20983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20984" type="x-p"/> And my portion - Allusion is here made to the division of the promised land. I ask no inheritance below; I look for one above. I do not look for this in the possession of any place; it is God alone that can content the desires and wishes of an immortal spirit. And even this would not satisfy, had I not the prospect of its being for ever, לעולם leolum, "to eternity!'
entries.8f51b106ea3ab7d17e6e9531c99a997bb3d73364: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen20984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20985" type="x-p"/> They that are far from thee shall perish - The term perish is generally used to signify a coming to nothing, being annihilated; and by some it is thus applied to the finally impenitent, they shall all be annihilated. But where is this to be found in the Scriptures? In no part, properly understood. In the new heavens and the new earth none of the wicked shall be found; for therein dwells righteousness - nothing but God and righteous spirits; but at the same time the wicked shall be in their own place. And to suppose that they shall be annihilated, is as great a heresy, though scarcely so absurd, as to believe that the pains of damnation are emendatory, and that hellfire shall burn out. There is presumptive evidence from Scripture to lead us to the conclusion, that if there be not eternal punishment, glory will not be eternal; as the same terms are used to express the duration of both. No human spirit that is not united to God can be saved. Those who are Far from Thee shall perish - they shall be lost, undone, ruined, and that without remedy. Being separated from God by sin, they shall never be rejoined; the great gulf must be between them and their Maker eternally. <div eID="gen20985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20986" type="x-p"/> All them that go a whoring from thee - That is, all that worship false gods; all idolaters. This is the only meaning of the word in such a connection. I have explained this elsewhere.
entries.2e4ca5e2824f2447fb6545c6746744f24cfbca92: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen20986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20987" type="x-p"/> It is good for me to draw near - We have already seen that those who are far off shall perish; therefore, it is ill for them. Those who draw near - who come in the true spirit of sacrifice, and with the only available offering, the Lord Jesus, shall be finally saved; therefore, it is good for them. <div eID="gen20987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20988" type="x-p"/> I have put my trust in the Lord God - I confide in Jehovah, my Prop and Stay. I have taken him for my portion. <div eID="gen20988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20989" type="x-p"/> That I may declare all thy works - That I may testify to all how good it is to draw nigh to God; and what a sufficient portion he is to the soul of man. <div eID="gen20989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20990" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, add, in the gates of the daughter of Sion. These words appear to make a better finish; but they are not acknowledged by any Hebrew MS.  <chapter eID="Ps.73"/> <div eID="gen20990" type="x-p"/>
